Field studies of Cochero (Dules auriga) in the coastal waters of southern Brazil have provided detailed insights into its reproductive physiology and life-history scheduling. At a stable water temperature of 13.2 °C [T = 13.2 °C], adult fish exhibited a gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 3% [GSI = 3%]. Histological examinations of gonad tissue from field-collected specimens confirmed that vitellogenic oocytes and active spermatogenic lobules were present only during the austral spring months, corroborating the seasonal nature of gamete production.

Analysis of length-frequency distributions from extensive trawl surveys allowed the estimation of key size thresholds for Cochero. The total length at which 50% of individuals are considered mature is 14.1 cm [Lp = 14.1 cm], indicating that puberty is reached at a relatively modest size. This value is roughly two-thirds of the species' ultimate total length, which was determined from the largest individuals encountered during the sampling program to be 19.5 cm [Li = 19.5 cm]. Such a size at puberty, representing a substantial fraction of the asymptotic length, is consistent with a life-history strategy that delays reproductive maturity until a significant portion of the growth trajectory has been completed. This pattern is common among temperate fishes, where the risk of predation on smaller adults and the energetic demands of gonadal development favor a later onset of maturity. The length-weight relationship derived from the same dataset indicates a strong positive allometry, with heavier individuals achieving a greater condition factor.

The relationship between length and wet weight, established from a large sample of individuals across all size classes, follows a power function that allowed the calculation of mass at various life stages. At birth, a newly hatched yolk-sac larva has an estimated wet weight of 0.00052 g [Wwb = 0.00052 g], a value derived from the average diameter of a mature egg, which is approximately 1 mm. This initial mass is remarkably small, reflecting the high fecundity typical of pelagic spawners that produce numerous, tiny offspring. An individual that has reached the length at puberty of 14.1 cm would be expected to weigh approximately 36 g [Wwp = approximately 36 g], based on the same predictive allometric equation. This mass at the onset of reproductive capability represents a several-thousand-fold increase from the larval stage, highlighting the extreme growth requirements of the juvenile phase. The ultimate wet weight for a fully grown adult, corresponding to the maximum observed total length of 19.5 cm, was calculated to be 98 g [Wwi = 98 g].

Early life history events in Cochero are tightly linked to thermal conditions in the nursery grounds. At a water temperature of 13.2 °C [T = 13.2 °C], the incubation period from fertilisation to hatching of the yolk-sac larva lasts approximately 5 days [ab = approximately 5 days], a duration that is typical for temperate marine teleosts with demersal or semi-buoyant eggs. This rapid embryonic development under cool conditions suggests a degree of physiological adaptation to the local thermal regime, allowing for successful recruitment even during the colder months. After hatching, the lecithotrophic larva relies entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves for roughly the first week of exogenous life. The transition to first feeding is a critical bottleneck, and the small, 0.00052 g hatchling must successfully capture planktonic prey to survive beyond the point of no return. The relatively short incubation period minimizes the time the vulnerable, incubating egg is exposed to benthic predators, a clear selective advantage. These early developmental rates are congruent with data from other locally adapted serranid populations.

Longevity records for Cochero, compiled from tag-recapture studies and validated through otolith annulus readings, reveal a maximum lifespan of approximately 11 years [am = approximately 11 years] when individuals are maintained under natural thermal conditions averaging 13.2 °C [T = 13.2 °C]. This extended lifespan, when paired with a moderate age at puberty of around 14.1 cm [Lp = around 14.1 cm] total length, paints a picture of a slow-paced life history relative to many other small-bodied teleosts. The species’ ultimate total length of 19.5 cm [Li = 19.5 cm] is attained relatively late in life, suggesting that growth continues well after sexual maturity. Such a pattern implies that older, larger females may contribute disproportionately to population fecundity through increased egg production, as is common in other iteroparous fishes. This longevity, however, also renders the population potentially vulnerable to overexploitation, as the replacement rate is low.
